messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Auditor
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 43

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Moral Violation: People misbehaving, Relationship Reminders: When people say things like my ex
  Maladaptive Strategies: Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit, Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance, Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kareem is a 22-year-old Lebanese American man who works as a junior auditor at a mid-sized accounting firm in a large Midwestern city. He was referred for psychological assessment following a disclosure to his university's counseling center, where he had briefly enrolled in a graduate certificate program while working full-time. He presented as guarded but articulate, and it took two sessions before he was willing to describe in any detail what had happened to him approximately eight months prior.

The assault occurred at a small gathering hosted by a man Kareem had been dating for several weeks. The apartment was unfamiliar to him — a detail that still sits heavily in his mind — and he had arrived feeling relaxed, carrying with him the particular ease of early romance. At some point during the evening, after the other guests had left, his partner became coercive and then physically forceful. Kareem remembered the smell of the man's cologne, something cedar-forward and expensive, and the way the apartment's overhead light had stayed on the entire time. He did not fight back in the way he later believed he should have. He left before dawn and told no one.

In the weeks that followed, Kareem found himself unable to account for what had happened in any way that felt tolerable. He had come to believe, with a quiet and persistent certainty, that someone else — someone more streetwise, more assertive, less trusting — would never have ended up in that situation. This thought was not occasional; it was structural, woven into how he understood himself. Alongside it lived a sense of humiliation that he experienced not as an emotion that might pass but as a permanent condition, something now stamped into who he was. He had been, before all of this, someone who laughed easily and made friends without effort. He was certain that person was gone.

The cologne was the first trigger he identified, though he did not initially connect it to the assault. He began noticing that certain men at his office wore similar fragrances, and that when the scent reached him in a conference room or elevator, his body responded before his mind caught up — shoulders locking, breath shortening, a flood of something he could not name. He started arriving early to meetings so he could choose a seat near the door, a habit he maintained with such consistency that a colleague jokingly remarked on it. He laughed it off, but the comment unsettled him. Being noticed was precisely what he was working to prevent. He had begun wearing darker, looser clothing to the office — dress shirts a size too large, jackets he didn't need in the summer — because he had decided, on some level he couldn't fully articulate, that drawing less attention to his body made him safer.

The auditing work itself became a source of dread. Performance reviews, client presentations, any moment in which his work or his appearance was being assessed sent him into a state of rigid self-monitoring that left him exhausted by midday. He began declining assignments that involved site visits to client offices he hadn't been to before, telling his supervisor he had scheduling conflicts. He had stopped being able to assess unfamiliar environments quickly enough to feel safe in them, and so he avoided them entirely. When colleagues made sudden movements — reaching across him for a document, standing up quickly from a chair — his body registered it as threat before any conscious thought intervened. He remained tense throughout the workday in a way that had become so familiar it no longer felt abnormal to him.

The final precipitating factor for seeking help was a conversation with a coworker who mentioned an ex-partner in passing, using a phrase — something like "my ex always said" — that collapsed the distance Kareem had been carefully maintaining between his present life and what had happened. He sat in the men's restroom for twenty minutes afterward, unable to return to his desk. That evening he made the appointment.

What he is most afraid of, he said in their third session, is that therapy will require him to say out loud what he has not yet been able to say to himself. What he is most hoping for, though he offered this quietly and without much confidence, is to feel like himself again — the person he used to be before happiness stopped being something he could access.
